chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Hisham ibn Salim from Malik ibn A'yan from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said:

I asked him about a Christian who died, leaving a Muslim son of his brother and a Muslim son of his sister, and the Christian had children and a Christian wife. He said, 'I see that the Muslim son of his brother should be given two-thirds of what he left, and the Muslim son of his sister should be given one-third of what he left, if he did not have young children. If he had young children, then the two heirs must spend from what they inherited from their father on the young children until they come of age.'

It was said to him, 'How do they spend?' He said, 'The heir of the two-thirds takes two-thirds of the maintenance, and the heir of the one-third takes one-third of the maintenance. When they come of age, they cease the maintenance for them.'

It was said to him, 'What if the children convert to Islam while they are young?' He said, 'What their father left is deposited with the Imam until they come of age. If they remain upon Islam, the Imam returns their inheritance to them. If they do not remain upon Islam when they come of age, the Imam returns the inheritance to the Muslim son of his brother and the Muslim son of his sister; he gives the son of the brother two-thirds of what was left and the son of the sister one-third of what was left.'

key_terms.الْإِمَام: the Imam (in this context, the authority holding the estate)

ai.seo_question: How is the estate of a Christian distributed among Muslim heirs when there are also Christian children involved?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* details the specific inheritance distribution for a Christian deceased, where Muslim cousins inherit the entire estate rather than the Christian children, reflecting the Shia principle of *kafā'ah* (compatibility) in inheritance. It further elaborates on the financial obligations of these Muslim heirs to maintain the Christian children until maturity, with the Imam overseeing the final disposition of the estate based on the children's religious status at adulthood. This ruling highlights the dynamic nature of inheritance rights in Shia jurisprudence, contingent upon the religious affiliation of the heirs.
